views.name: cleaned_weekly_sales_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  week_date_formatted AS week_date_formatted,
  week_date AS week_date,
  region AS region,
  platform AS platform,
  segment AS segment,
  customer_type AS customer_type,
  transactions AS transactions,
  sales AS sales,
  week_number AS week_number,
  month_number AS month_number,
  calendar_year AS calendar_year,
  age_band AS age_band,
  demographic AS demographic,
  avg_transaction AS avg_transaction
FROM cleaned_weekly_sales

params.description: Weekly-level cleaned sales and transaction metrics by week_date_formatted, region, platform, segment, and customer_type.
params.when_to_use: Report weekly sales trends and transaction counts by region, platform, customer segment, or customer type. | Compose higher-level time-series (weekly) analyses such as rolling averages, week-over-week growth, or joins to calendar/date dimensions. | Filter or aggregate these weekly measures up to month_number or calendar_year and combine with other weekly-level metrics.
params.output_schema: week_date_formatted: human-readable week label (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.week_date_formatted) | week_date: canonical week start (date) used as the week key (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.week_date) | region: geographic region for the metric (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.region) | platform: platform/channel (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.platform) | segment: customer or product segment (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.segment) | customer_type: classification of customer (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.customer_type) | transactions: number of transactions in the week at this grain (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.transactions) | sales: total sales (monetary) in the week at this grain (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.sales) | week_number: numeric week of year for the week_date (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.week_number) | month_number: numeric month for the week_date (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.month_number) | calendar_year: calendar year for the week_date (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.calendar_year) | age_band: demographic age bucket for the cohort at this row (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.age_band) | demographic: demographic dimension value (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.demographic) | avg_transaction: average transaction value (derived from cleaned_weekly_sales.avg_transaction)
params.grounded_columns: cleaned_weekly_sales.week_date_formatted | cleaned_weekly_sales.week_date | cleaned_weekly_sales.region | cleaned_weekly_sales.platform | cleaned_weekly_sales.segment | cleaned_weekly_sales.customer_type | cleaned_weekly_sales.transactions | cleaned_weekly_sales.sales | cleaned_weekly_sales.week_number | cleaned_weekly_sales.month_number | cleaned_weekly_sales.calendar_year | cleaned_weekly_sales.age_band | cleaned_weekly_sales.demographic | cleaned_weekly_sales.avg_transaction
params.metric: transactions = cleaned_weekly_sales.transactions  -- raw count of transactions at the view grain | sales = cleaned_weekly_sales.sales  -- raw sum of sales (monetary) at the view grain | avg_transaction = cleaned_weekly_sales.avg_transaction  -- pre-computed average transaction value at the view grain
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a date/calendar dimension on week_date (e.g., calendar.week_date = cleaned_weekly_sales.week_date) — safe because calendar is one-row-per-week, so it does not duplicate measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to region lookup/dimension on region (e.g., region_dim.region = cleaned_weekly_sales.region) — safe if the region dimension is one-row-per-region; measures remain unduplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to platform or customer_type dimension on platform or customer_type respectively — safe when those dimensions are one-row-per-key. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many detail tables (for example, transactional-level tables or event logs such as shopping_cart_events_with_page) without re-aggregating the detail to this view's grain first, because such joins would multiply transactions and sales. If you must combine with a one-to-many table, pre-aggregate that table to the keys (week_date or week_date_formatted, region, platform, segment, customer_type) and then join on those keys. | do NOT join to sibling JOIN or RANK views that are many-to-one into cleaned_weekly_sales unless you can guarantee they are one-row-per (week_date, region, platform, segment, customer_type). If a sibling view contains multiple rows per this view's grain, you must aggregate the sibling view to this grain prior to joining. | If composing metrics (summing or averaging): to aggregate up to a higher grain (e.g., month_number or calendar_year), SUM(transactions) and SUM(sales) are safe. For avg_transaction at higher grain, compute a weighted average: SUM(sales) / NULLIF(SUM(transactions),0) rather than AVG(avg_transaction) to avoid incorrect weighting.

views.description: Normalized/cleaned weekly sales rows with canonical date parts and preserved identifiers. Use this as the canonical cleaned weekly sales relation for time-series, aggregation, and joins. Parses week_date_formatted/week_date into ISO-like text where possible and exposes calendar_year, month_number, week_number and avg_transaction as-is. | Use for: time series of sales or transactions by region/platform/segment/customer_type; average transaction amount trends by demographic or age_band; year-over-year or month-over-month comparisons at weekly granularity

views.name: weekly_sales_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  week_date AS week_date,
  region AS region,
  platform AS platform,
  segment AS segment,
  customer_type AS customer_type,
  transactions AS transactions,
  sales AS sales
FROM weekly_sales

params.description: Week-level aggregated sales and transaction counts broken down by week_date, region, platform, segment, and customer_type.
params.when_to_use: Report total sales and number of transactions per week per region/platform/segment/customer_type. | Build higher-level aggregates (e.g., monthly, regional totals) by summing these weekly measures. | Join to dimension data (e.g., region or platform lookup) that is one-row-per-key to enrich labels without duplicating measures. | Use as a base for time-series analyses (e.g., trend, moving averages) at the weekly grain defined.
params.output_schema: week_date: week start date of the reporting week — derived directly from weekly_sales.week_date | region: geographic region label — derived directly from weekly_sales.region | platform: platform identifier (e.g., web, mobile) — derived directly from weekly_sales.platform | segment: customer or product segment label — derived directly from weekly_sales.segment | customer_type: classification of customer (e.g., new, returning) — derived directly from weekly_sales.customer_type | transactions: count of transactions in that week for the given combination — derived directly from weekly_sales.transactions | sales: total sales amount in that week for the given combination — derived directly from weekly_sales.sales
params.grounded_columns: weekly_sales.week_date | weekly_sales.region | weekly_sales.platform | weekly_sales.segment | weekly_sales.customer_type | weekly_sales.transactions | weekly_sales.sales
params.metric: transactions = weekly_sales.transactions  -- measure present at the view grain; treat as an additive integer/count measure across the view's grain | sales = weekly_sales.sales  -- measure present at the view grain; treat as an additive numeric measure (currency) across the view's grain
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to one-row-per-key dimension views/tables on matching keys without duplicating measures. Examples: |   - Join to a region dimension (e.g., regions_dim) on weekly_sales_base.region = regions_dim.region_id — safe because regions_dim should be one row per region so transactions/sales remain at one row per original weekly_sales_base grain. |   - Join to a platform dimension (e.g., platforms_dim) on weekly_sales_base.platform = platforms_dim.platform_id — safe when platforms_dim is one-row-per-platform. |   - Join to a segment lookup on weekly_sales_base.segment = segments_dim.segment_id — safe when segments_dim is one-row-per-segment. | Do NOT join this view directly to one-to-many detail tables or views (these would multiply this view's rows and therefore incorrectly inflate transactions/sales) unless you first re-aggregate the detail to the same grouping keys (week_date, region, platform, segment, customer_type). Examples of unsafe joins without re-aggregation: |   - Do NOT join to shopping_cart_events_with_page or shopping_cart_events_ranked directly on customer or cookie keys because those are event-level or multi-row per customer and would duplicate weekly metrics. |   - Do NOT join to bitcoin_transactions_enriched, veg_txn_base, customer_transactions_base, or any transaction-level table/view directly without first aggregating them to (week_date, region, platform, segment, customer_type), because they are one-to-many relative to this weekly grain. | Safe pattern to combine with one-to-many sources: aggregate the detail to the same grain and then join. Example plan: |   1) Aggregate shopping_cart_events_with_page to (week_date, region, platform, segment, customer_type) summing events or counts needed. |   2) LEFT JOIN the aggregated results to weekly_sales_base on all five keys — this preserves cardinality and allows correct additive combination of metrics. | If you need to enrich by attributes that are many-to-one to this view (e.g., mapping each customer_type to a single lifecycle bucket), those joins are safe because they do not duplicate rows.

views.description: Base pass-through view of weekly_sales preserving original columns. Use when the raw weekly_sales table is needed for comparisons or where cleaned_weekly_sales is not used. | Use for: raw weekly sales inspections; comparing raw and cleaned weekly sales; cohort selection by customer_type/segment/platform

views.name: bitcoin_transactions_enriched
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  b.txn_id AS txn_id,
  b.member_id AS member_id,
  m.first_name AS first_name,
  m.region AS region,
  b.ticker AS ticker,
  b.txn_date AS txn_date,
  b.txn_time AS txn_time,
  b.txn_type AS txn_type,
  b.quantity AS quantity,
  b.percentage_fee AS percentage_fee
FROM bitcoin_transactions b
LEFT JOIN bitcoin_members m
  ON b.member_id = m.member_id

params.description: Enriched, one-row-per-transaction view combining bitcoin_transactions with member attributes to answer transaction-level queries about who, what, when, and fee/quantity details.
params.when_to_use: Get transaction-level details (txn_id) with member attributes for reporting or further aggregation (e.g., counts, sums by member, region, ticker, date). | Build aggregations of transaction metrics (sum quantity, avg percentage_fee) grouped by member, region, ticker, date, or txn_type. | Filter transactions by member attributes (first_name, region) while preserving transaction grain. | Join to price or running-total views keyed by date/ticker or to other 1:1 dimension-like views for enrichment.
params.output_schema: txn_id: transaction identifier — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_id (base table). This is the row-level grain. | member_id: member identifier who executed the transaction — derived from bitcoin_transactions.member_id (base table). | first_name: member's first name for the member_id — derived from bitcoin_members.first_name (joined table). May be NULL if member missing. | region: member's region for the member_id — derived from bitcoin_members.region (joined table). May be NULL if member missing. | ticker: asset ticker symbol traded in the transaction — derived from bitcoin_transactions.ticker (base table). | txn_date: transaction date (date) — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_date (base table). | txn_time: transaction time (time or timestamp) — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_time (base table). | txn_type: transaction type (e.g., BUY/SELL) — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_type (base table). | quantity: quantity traded in the transaction — derived from bitcoin_transactions.quantity (base table). | percentage_fee: percentage fee applied to the transaction — derived from bitcoin_transactions.percentage_fee (base table).
params.grounded_columns: bitcoin_transactions.txn_id | bitcoin_transactions.member_id | bitcoin_transactions.ticker | bitcoin_transactions.txn_date | bitcoin_transactions.txn_time | bitcoin_transactions.txn_type | bitcoin_transactions.quantity | bitcoin_transactions.percentage_fee | bitcoin_members.member_id | bitcoin_members.first_name | bitcoin_members.region
params.metric: quantity = bitcoin_transactions.quantity  -- base numeric measure at txn_id grain (not an aggregate in this view) | percentage_fee = bitcoin_transactions.percentage_fee  -- base numeric measure at txn_id grain (not an aggregate in this view) | count_txn = 1  -- implicit row-count when aggregating this view (use COUNT(*) or COUNT(txn_id))
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to member-like dimension views (e.g., bitcoin_members or other one-row-per-member views) on member_id — safe because bitcoin_transactions_enriched is one-row-per-txn and the member dimension is one-row-per-member, so joining will not duplicate transaction rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to bitcoin_prices_daily on (ticker, txn_date) — safe when bitcoin_prices_daily is one-row-per-(ticker,txn_date), because each transaction matches at most one price row and transaction measures (quantity, percentage_fee) will not be duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to bitcoin_transactions_running_totals on txn_id or on (member_id, txn_date, txn_time) only if that sibling view provides a one-row-per-txn mapping (verify its grain) — safe when it is one-row-per-txn; otherwise do not join directly. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views (e.g., an events table with multiple rows per txn_id or a shopping_cart_events_with_page if many events map to a single txn) without first aggregating those tables to txn_id-level. Joining a one-to-many child will multiply this view's transaction rows and thereby double-count quantity and percentage_fee when aggregating. | when composing aggregations: if you need aggregated measures from a one-to-many child, first compute aggregates (SUM, COUNT, AVG) grouped by txn_id, then LEFT JOIN that aggregated result to bitcoin_transactions_enriched on txn_id to preserve correct measure cardinality. | if joining to sibling aggregated views (e.g., interest_metrics_by_interest or weekly_sales_base), ensure the sibling view's grain is compatible: join only when the sibling is at the same txn-level or pre-aggregated to the grouping keys you plan to use; otherwise aggregate sibling first. | example safe composition patterns: 1) To compute total quantity by region and date — aggregate bitcoin_transactions_enriched: GROUP BY region, txn_date SUM(quantity). 2) To add price-based USD value per txn — LEFT JOIN bitcoin_prices_daily (ticker, txn_date) and compute quantity * price. 3) To include per-txn running totals — LEFT JOIN bitcoin_transactions_running_totals if that view is one-row-per-txn on txn_id.

views.description: Bitcoin transactions enriched with member first_name and member region where available. Preserves txn-level grain and exposes transaction measures for downstream aggregation or member-level analysis. | Use for: member-level bitcoin activity; volume and fee summaries by member or region; time series of txn quantities for tickers or member segments

views.name: bitcoin_prices_daily
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ticker AS ticker,
  market_date AS market_date,
  price AS price,
  open AS open,
  high AS high,
  low AS low,
  volume AS volume,
  change AS change
FROM bitcoin_prices

params.description: Daily per-ticker price and volume metrics for bitcoin-derived tickers on each market_date.
params.when_to_use: Get the daily price, open, high, low, volume, and change for a specific ticker on a specific date. | Trend analysis: compose daily price series for time-series charts or aggregations (e.g., weekly/monthly) by grouping market_date. | Join as a facts table to enrich user/transaction records with the day's bitcoin price for the ticker and date. | Compute derived metrics (e.g., VWAP-like approximations, percent change over a period) by aggregating the daily rows.
params.output_schema: ticker: the ticker identifier for the bitcoin instrument (derived from bitcoin_prices.ticker) | market_date: the calendar date of the price observation (derived from bitcoin_prices.market_date) | price: closing or reported price for that ticker on market_date (derived from bitcoin_prices.price) | open: opening price for that ticker on market_date (derived from bitcoin_prices.open) | high: highest price observed for that ticker on market_date (derived from bitcoin_prices.high) | low: lowest price observed for that ticker on market_date (derived from bitcoin_prices.low) | volume: traded volume for that ticker on market_date (derived from bitcoin_prices.volume) | change: price change metric for that ticker on market_date (derived from bitcoin_prices.change)
params.grounded_columns: bitcoin_prices.ticker | bitcoin_prices.market_date | bitcoin_prices.price | bitcoin_prices.open | bitcoin_prices.high | bitcoin_prices.low | bitcoin_prices.volume | bitcoin_prices.change
params.metric: price = identity(bitcoin_prices.price) | open = identity(bitcoin_prices.open) | high = identity(bitcoin_prices.high) | low = identity(bitcoin_prices.low) | volume = identity(bitcoin_prices.volume) | change = identity(bitcoin_prices.change)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension tables or views keyed 1:1 to (ticker, market_date) — e.g., if there existed a per-ticker-per-date metadata view keyed by (ticker, market_date), joining on (ticker, market_date) is safe because bitcoin_prices_daily is defined at one row per (ticker, market_date) and such a join would not multiply rows. | safe to join to daily-level views aggregated to (ticker, market_date) (or to a single-row-per-ticker table) on matching keys because those sources are 1:1 with this view's grain. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables or views (for example: raw transactions, multiple events per day, or any view that has many rows per (ticker, market_date)) without first aggregating the other side to (ticker, market_date) or using an appropriate DISTINCT/ROW_NUMBER reduction. Such joins will multiply the bitcoin_prices_daily measures (price, volume, etc.) and produce incorrect totals. | when composing higher-level aggregates (weekly, monthly): aggregate bitcoin_prices_daily (e.g., SUM(volume) for total volume; AVG(price) or weighted averages if desired) rather than joining bitcoin_prices_daily to a lower-grain table and then aggregating, to preserve correct measure semantics. | example safe composition patterns: 1) to compute weekly total volume per ticker, GROUP BY ticker and week(market_date) over bitcoin_prices_daily and SUM(volume). 2) to enrich a transaction dataset that has one row per transaction, first aggregate transactions to (ticker, market_date) (e.g., COUNT(*), SUM(txn_value)) then join aggregated transactions to bitcoin_prices_daily on (ticker, market_date). | explicit join keys: join on bitcoin_prices_daily.ticker = <other>.ticker AND bitcoin_prices_daily.market_date = <other>.market_date for 1:1 or many-to-1 (other -> this) safe joins; avoid joining where bitcoin_prices_daily would act as the 'one' side and the other table is also many-to-many without prior aggregation.

views.description: Canonical daily bitcoin prices relation (one row per ticker/market_date) preserving price, open/high/low and volume/change as provided. Use for price time-series and joins to transaction dates after parsing. | Use for: historical price lookups by ticker and date; join prices to transactions by date to compute P&L or price at txn date

views.name: shopping_cart_events_with_page
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  e.visit_id AS visit_id,
  e.cookie_id AS cookie_id,
  e.page_id AS page_id,
  p.page_name AS page_name,
  p.product_category AS product_category,
  p.product_id AS product_id,
  e.event_type AS event_type,
  e.sequence_number AS sequence_number,
  e.event_time AS event_time
FROM shopping_cart_events e
LEFT JOIN shopping_cart_page_hierarchy p
  ON e.page_id = p.page_id

params.description: Provides one row per shopping cart event enriched with page metadata (page name and product category) to analyze event sequences within visits.
params.when_to_use: Find or filter individual shopping cart events (e.g., clicks, adds, removes) by visit, page, product, or time. | Analyze event sequences within a visit (order of events via sequence_number) and correlate events with page attributes. | Compose higher-level aggregations: counts of events per visit, events per page, events per product category, or event funnels by page or product. | Join with user-level or session-level tables keyed by visit_id or cookie_id to enrich events with user/session attributes (ensuring correct cardinality handling).
params.output_schema: visit_id: identifier for the visit from shopping_cart_events.visit_id | cookie_id: cookie identifier from shopping_cart_events.cookie_id | page_id: page identifier from shopping_cart_events.page_id | page_name: human-readable page name from shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.page_name | product_category: product category for the page from shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.product_category | product_id: product identifier from shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.product_id | event_type: type of the event (e.g., add, remove, view) from shopping_cart_events.event_type | sequence_number: event sequence within the visit from shopping_cart_events.sequence_number | event_time: event timestamp from shopping_cart_events.event_time
params.grounded_columns: shopping_cart_events.visit_id | shopping_cart_events.cookie_id | shopping_cart_events.page_id | shopping_cart_events.event_type | shopping_cart_events.sequence_number | shopping_cart_events.event_time | shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.page_id | shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.page_name | shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.product_category | shopping_cart_page_hierarchy.product_id
params.metric: row_count = count(*) OVER ()  -- implicit row enumerator; view is at event grain (visit_id, sequence_number) | event_exists = 1  -- each row represents a single event; can be aggregated (sum(event_exists)) to count events | event_time = shopping_cart_events.event_time  -- timestamp metric for time-based analyses (min/max/avg over groups)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to session- or user-level one-row-per-key dimensions on visit_id or cookie_id — e.g., join to shopping_cart_users_cookie_map on cookie_id (safe because shopping_cart_users_cookie_map is expected to be one-row-per-cookie, so it will not duplicate events). | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to shopping_cart_events_ranked on (visit_id, sequence_number) only if that sibling view is one-row-per-(visit_id,sequence_number) (safe if ranking produced unique rows per event); verify its uniqueness before joining. | do NOT join directly to any one-to-many detail (e.g., a table that has multiple rows per (visit_id, sequence_number) such as event-attribute lookup or multi-valued tags) without first aggregating those details to the event grain — such joins would duplicate event rows and inflate counts/measures. | do NOT join to shopping_cart_events (base) again in a way that creates a second matching row per (visit_id,sequence_number) — the view already sources from shopping_cart_events and is at that event-level grain. | safe-aggregation pattern: when composing metrics, aggregate at the view's grain first (GROUP BY visit_id, sequence_number) or use SUM(event_exists) after joining external dimensions that are one-to-one with visit_id or cookie_id. | example safe join keys: ON view.visit_id = other_session_view.visit_id (if other_session_view is one-row-per-visit), ON view.cookie_id = shopping_cart_users_cookie_map.cookie_id (one-row-per-cookie). | example unsafe joins to avoid without re-aggregation: joining to a purchases table that can have multiple purchase rows per visit_id or multiple product impressions per page_id — either pre-aggregate those tables to one-row-per-visit or one-row-per-event, or perform aggregations after joining using DISTINCT keys to avoid double-counting.

views.description: Enriched shopping cart events with page metadata (page_name, product_category, product_id). Preserves event-level grain and sequence_number for session reconstruction and funnel analysis. | Use for: session funnel and sequence analysis; page-level conversion and drop-off analysis; linking events to product categories for campaign analysis

views.name: shopping_cart_users_cookie_map
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  user_id AS user_id,
  cookie_id AS cookie_id,
  start_date AS start_date
FROM shopping_cart_users

params.description: Maps each shopping-cart user to the cookie that first/last (as recorded) associated with them and the date that association started.
params.when_to_use: Look up the cookie_id associated with a given user_id | Join user-level cookie identifiers into downstream analyses (daily attribution, user-session linking) without changing user grain | Filter or group other datasets to the set of users present in shopping_cart_users
params.output_schema: user_id: unique identifier for a user — derived directly from shopping_cart_users.user_id | cookie_id: cookie identifier associated with the user — derived directly from shopping_cart_users.cookie_id | start_date: date when the cookie association for this user started (as recorded) — derived directly from shopping_cart_users.start_date
params.metric: This view exposes no aggregated metrics. All columns are direct passthroughs (no expressions or aggregates): | user_id = shopping_cart_users.user_id | cookie_id = shopping_cart_users.cookie_id | start_date = shopping_cart_users.start_date
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension or lookup tables that are one-row-per-user (for example, a canonical users table keyed by user_id) on user_id — safe because shopping_cart_users_cookie_map is one-row-per-user_id (grain = ['user_id']), so its user-level attributes will not be duplicated. | Safe to JOIN (one-to-one or many-to-one from this view's perspective): join to cleaned_weekly_sales_base, weekly_sales_base, customer_transactions_base, or other user-grain views/tables ON user_id — these joins will not multiply rows if the target is many-records-per-user only when you aggregate the target to user level first. | Do NOT join directly (inner/left) to inherently one-to-many child tables or views such as shopping_cart_events_with_page, shopping_cart_events_ranked, veg_txn_base, or bitcoin_transactions_enriched without first aggregating those tables up to user_id — joining them directly will multiply this view's rows and thus duplicate any measures if you treat cookie_id/start_date as measures. | If you need event-level rows that include cookie_id, perform the join from the event table to this view (event_table LEFT JOIN shopping_cart_users_cookie_map USING (user_id)) — that is safe because you are expanding events with a user-level attribute; ensure you do not aggregate post-join expecting the view to be at event grain unless you re-aggregate appropriately. | When composing metrics: if you aggregate after joining a one-to-many source, always aggregate the one-to-many source first (e.g., count of events per user) and then join to this view, or use DISTINCT/ROW_NUMBER patterns on the one-to-many side to preserve cardinality. | Summary: this view is authoritative at the user_id grain; joins that preserve user_id as unique (one-row-per-user) are safe. Any join that would create multiple rows per user must be followed by re-aggregation to avoid duplicating user-level attributes.

views.description: Mapping of shopping cart users to cookie_id and start_date. Use this to join cookie-based events to user identifiers and compute user cohorts by start_date. | Use for: attributing events/sessions to users; user cohort analysis from start_date; cross-system linking when cookie_id matches other member ids

views.name: interest_metrics_by_interest
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  interest_id AS interest_id,
  month_year AS month_year,
  _month AS _month,
  _year AS _year,
  composition AS composition,
  index_value AS index_value,
  ranking AS ranking,
  percentile_ranking AS percentile_ranking
FROM interest_metrics

params.description: Provides monthly interest-level metrics (composition, index, rank, percentile) per interest_id and month_year.
params.when_to_use: Get time-series metrics for a specific interest (month granularity) for reporting or trend analysis | Rank or compare interests within a given month (e.g., top-N interests by index_value or composition) | Join interest-month metrics into dashboards or to enrich dimension tables at the granularity interest_id × month_year | Use as an aggregated base when composing further aggregations (e.g., compute rolling averages across months) rather than re-aggregating raw events
params.output_schema: interest_id: identifier for the interest; derived directly from interest_metrics.interest_id | month_year: month identifier (likely YYYY-MM or similar) for the metric row; derived from interest_metrics.month_year | _month: numeric month (1-12) extracted/preserved from interest_metrics._month | _year: year value extracted/preserved from interest_metrics._year | composition: composition metric (a share/proportion or composition score) as stored in interest_metrics.composition | index_value: index metric (relative index or normalized score) as stored in interest_metrics.index_value | ranking: integer rank of the interest within the month as stored in interest_metrics.ranking | percentile_ranking: percentile rank (0-100 or 0-1 depending on upstream definition) as stored in interest_metrics.percentile_ranking
params.grounded_columns: interest_metrics.interest_id | interest_metrics.month_year | interest_metrics._month | interest_metrics._year | interest_metrics.composition | interest_metrics.index_value | interest_metrics.ranking | interest_metrics.percentile_ranking
params.metric: composition = composition (pass-through from interest_metrics.composition) | index_value = index_value (pass-through from interest_metrics.index_value) | ranking = ranking (pass-through from interest_metrics.ranking) | percentile_ranking = percentile_ranking (pass-through from interest_metrics.percentile_ranking)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to an interest dimension (e.g., interest_dimension) on interest_id — safe because this view is one-row-per interest_id × month_year so enriching with 1:1 or many-to-1 dimensions will not duplicate measures | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a month/calendar dimension on (month_year or (_year, _month)) — safe because calendar dimension is 1:1 per month identifier | do NOT join directly to any one-to-many fact/detail table (e.g., raw events, transactions) on interest_id or month_year without first aggregating that detail table to interest_id × month_year. Such joins would multiply rows and therefore duplicate composition/index_value/ranking measures | do NOT join to sibling aggregated views that are at a finer grain (many rows per interest_id × month_year) unless you aggregate the finer-grained data up to interest_id × month_year before joining | safe composition pattern examples: (1) derive a cross-interest comparison by joining this view (one row per interest_id×month_year) to an interest dimension to add names/labels; (2) compute a weighted average across interests by joining this view to another aggregated metric at the same grain (interest_id × month_year) — ensure both sides are same grain to avoid duplication | unsafe composition examples: joining directly to weekly_sales_base or cleaned_weekly_sales_base without pre-aggregating them to interest_id × month_year (they appear to be normalized at weekly or lower grain) because those tables are many-to-one relative to this view and will multiply this view's rows/metrics

views.description: Monthly interest metrics aggregated at interest_id/month_year grain, preserving index and composition measures along with ranking and percentile. Useful for time-series or ranking analyses of interests. | Use for: trend of index_value or composition for an interest; top-ranked interests by month/year using ranking or percentile_ranking

views.name: customer_transactions_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customer_id AS customer_id,
  txn_date AS txn_date,
  txn_type AS txn_type,
  txn_amount AS txn_amount
FROM customer_transactions

params.description: Row-level normalized transaction facts per customer, date, type, and amount — answers who did what transaction when and for how much.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve raw customer transactions for reporting or downstream aggregation (e.g., totals by customer, date, or type). | Use as a base to compute aggregated metrics such as total spend per customer, daily volume, or counts by transaction type. | Join to customer- or product-dimension tables to enrich transactions (ensuring join cardinality safety as described). | Feed into windowing or ranking transformations (e.g., running totals, rolling sums) keyed by customer and date.
params.output_schema: customer_id: unique identifier for the customer performing the transaction; derived directly from customer_transactions.customer_id | txn_date: date of the transaction; derived directly from customer_transactions.txn_date | txn_type: categorical type of the transaction (e.g., payment, refund); derived directly from customer_transactions.txn_type | txn_amount: monetary amount of the transaction; derived directly from customer_transactions.txn_amount
params.metric: txn_amount = raw measure (value from customer_transactions.txn_amount); NOT an aggregate in this base view | txn_count = 1 per output row (implicit row-level event count) — to produce aggregated counts, SUM(1) or COUNT(*) must be applied by the consumer | total_spend_by_agg = SUM(txn_amount) when the consumer aggregates this view by desired grouping (customer_id, txn_date, txn_type, etc.)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension/lookups that are one-to-one or many-to-one from this view's grain without re-aggregation. Example: join to a customer dimension on customer_id — safe because this view is one row per (customer_id, txn_date, txn_type, txn_amount) and the customer dimension is expected to have one row per customer_id, so measures (txn_amount, implicit txn_count) are not duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a transaction-type or code table on txn_type — safe when that table is one row per txn_type, preserving this view's measures. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables (which would duplicate measures) such as a shopping_cart_events table keyed to the same customer but having multiple events per transaction or per date, or any table that can have multiple rows for the same (customer_id, txn_date, txn_type) combination — if you must join to a one-to-many source, first aggregate that source to the same grain (customer_id, txn_date, txn_type) or to the join keys, or re-aggregate after the join to remove duplication. | do NOT join to sibling transaction-like bases (e.g., veg_txn_base) or event streams without aligning grain and re-aggregating; instead use UNION ALL of normalized bases where appropriate and then aggregate. | when composing with WINDOW or RANK views (e.g., computing running totals): partition/window by customer_id (and optionally txn_type) and order by txn_date — safe because this base provides the raw rows; ensure deterministic ordering when txn_date ties exist (include a tie-breaker if necessary). | when joining to enriched/joined views (e.g., bitcoin_transactions_enriched) verify their grain is one-to-one to this view on the join keys; if the enriched view is many-to-one toward this view it's safe, otherwise aggregate the enriched side first.

views.description: Base customer transactions relation preserving customer_id, txn_date, txn_type, and txn_amount for downstream aggregations (LTV, recency, frequency). | Use for: customer spend summaries and aggregates; recency-frequency-monetary (RFM) calculations; filtering deposits vs withdrawals and their totals

views.name: veg_txn_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  "index" AS "index",
  txn_date AS txn_date,
  txn_time AS txn_time,
  item_code AS item_code,
  "qty_sold(kg)" AS "qty_sold(kg)",
  "unit_selling_px_rmb/kg" AS "unit_selling_px_rmb/kg",
  "sale/return" AS "sale/return",
  "discount(%)" AS "discount(%)",
  day_of_week AS day_of_week
FROM veg_txn_df

params.description: A row-level normalized transaction feed of vegetable sales/returns at the per-transaction (index) grain, providing date/time, item, quantity (kg), unit price, sale vs return flag, discount percent, and weekday.
params.when_to_use: Answer transactional-level questions such as sales or returns for a given transaction index, item_code, date, or time. | Compose aggregate queries over transactions (e.g., total kg sold, average unit price, total transactions) by grouping this view. | Join to item master or customer/contextual dimensions when you need per-transaction detail before aggregation. | Build time-series or weekday analyses by aggregating txn_date or day_of_week from the base transaction rows.
params.output_schema: index: unique transaction row identifier at the view grain — derived from veg_txn_df."index" | txn_date: transaction date (date or date-string) — derived from veg_txn_df.txn_date | txn_time: transaction time (time or time-string) — derived from veg_txn_df.txn_time | item_code: item identifier (SKU/code) sold or returned — derived from veg_txn_df.item_code | qty_sold(kg): quantity sold in kilograms for this transaction row — derived from veg_txn_df."qty_sold(kg)" | unit_selling_px_rmb/kg: unit selling price in RMB per kg for this transaction row — derived from veg_txn_df."unit_selling_px_rmb/kg" | sale/return: indicator if this row is a sale or a return (value comes from source) — derived from veg_txn_df."sale/return" | discount(%): discount percentage applied to this transaction row — derived from veg_txn_df."discount(%)" | day_of_week: weekday of the transaction (e.g., Monday) — derived from veg_txn_df.day_of_week
params.grounded_columns: veg_txn_df."index" | veg_txn_df.txn_date | veg_txn_df.txn_time | veg_txn_df.item_code | veg_txn_df."qty_sold(kg)" | veg_txn_df."unit_selling_px_rmb/kg" | veg_txn_df."sale/return" | veg_txn_df."discount(%)" | veg_txn_df.day_of_week
params.metric: qty_sold_kg = qty_sold(kg)  -- atomic numeric measure available per row (no aggregation implied) | unit_price_rmb_per_kg = unit_selling_px_rmb/kg  -- atomic price measure per row | net_value_rmb = qty_sold(kg) * unit_selling_px_rmb/kg * (1 - coalesce("discount(%)",0)/100)  -- derived expression you can compute when aggregating (not present as a stored column in the view; compute in downstream SQL) | is_return = ("sale/return" = 'return' OR "sale/return" = 'R')  -- example boolean interpretation; downstream queries should use the actual values present
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to veg_item_master on item_code — safe because veg_item_master is expected to be one-row-per-item_code (dimension); joining will not duplicate veg_txn_base measures when veg_item_master.item_code is unique. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customer_transactions_base only if customer_transactions_base is one-row-per-transaction index on matching index — safe when the other view is a 1:1 enrichment keyed by index. | DO NOT join without care to one-to-many tables/views such as shopping_cart_events_with_page, shopping_cart_events_ranked, or any event-level tables that can have multiple rows per transaction index — such joins will multiply veg_txn_base rows and will duplicate measures (e.g., qty_sold(kg)). If you must join to a one-to-many source, first aggregate that source to the transaction index (or item_code + date, etc.) so it becomes one-row-per-index before joining. | When composing aggregates (SUM, AVG) over this view, aggregate qty_sold(kg) and compute net_value_rmb from the row expression (qty_sold(kg)*unit_selling_px_rmb/kg*(1-discount(%)/100)) before summing to avoid double-counting after joins. | Safe-time-series composition: to build daily aggregates, GROUP BY txn_date (or date-truncated txn_date) — this view is already at a transactional grain so grouping up is correct. | Avoid joining to sibling aggregated views (e.g., interest_metrics_by_interest, weekly_sales_base) without understanding their grain. If you join this transaction-level view to an aggregated view that is many-to-one to txn_date or item_code, prefer joining aggregated transaction results to that aggregated view at a common grain to prevent duplication.

views.description: Base vegetable transactions at the transaction row level preserving item_code, txn_date/txn_time, quantity and unit price and other provided fields. Useful for sales, volume, and day-of-week analyses. | Use for: per-item sales volume and revenue; weekday vs weekend sales comparisons; impact of discounts on qty_sold

views.name: veg_item_master
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.item_code AS item_code,
  c.item_name AS item_name,
  c.category_code AS category_code,
  c.category_name AS category_name,
  l."loss_rate_%" AS "loss_rate_%"
FROM veg_cat c
LEFT JOIN veg_loss_rate_df l
  ON c.item_code = l.item_code

params.description: Provides a master list of vegetable items with their category and associated loss rate percentage (if available).
params.when_to_use: Lookup an item's name, category, and loss rate by item_code | Enrich transactional or inventory data with item metadata and loss rate | Compose reports that need per-item loss percentage alongside item/category labels
params.output_schema: item_code: item identifier (from veg_cat.item_code) | item_name: human-readable item name (from veg_cat.item_name) | category_code: category identifier for the item (from veg_cat.category_code) | category_name: human-readable category name (from veg_cat.category_name) | loss_rate_%: loss rate percentage for the item (from veg_loss_rate_df."loss_rate_%")
params.grounded_columns: veg_cat.item_code | veg_cat.item_name | veg_cat.category_code | veg_cat.category_name | veg_loss_rate_df.item_code | veg_loss_rate_df."loss_rate_%"
params.metric: loss_rate_% = veg_loss_rate_df."loss_rate_%" (direct passthrough; no aggregation in this view)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension or lookup tables on item_code (for example, join to other per-item master views keyed by item_code) — safe because veg_item_master is one-row-per-item_code as defined by veg_cat (LEFT JOIN to veg_loss_rate_df does not create duplicates when veg_cat.item_code is unique). | do NOT join veg_item_master directly to one-to-many event/transaction tables (e.g., veg_txn_base, cleaned_weekly_sales_base, weekly_sales_base, customer_transactions_base) without aggregation on the transaction side first, because those tables contain multiple rows per item_code and would multiply rows/measures from veg_item_master if the planner expects aggregated measures. | If you need item-level metrics combined with transactional aggregates, first aggregate transactions to item_code (e.g., SUM(quantity) GROUP BY item_code) and then join the aggregated result to veg_item_master on item_code — this preserves correct cardinality and prevents double-counting. | Joining to other one-row-per-item sources (or other single-row-per-key views) on item_code is safe (e.g., another master lookup that guarantees uniqueness on item_code). | Avoid joining to tables where uniqueness on item_code is not guaranteed (e.g., shopping_cart_events_with_page, shopping_cart_events_ranked, veg_txn_base) unless those sides are reduced to one row per item_code via aggregation or distinct selection beforehand.

views.description: Vegetable item master by joining category and loss-rate info to provide descriptive attributes for item_code. Preserves item_code as key and exposes item_name, category_name and loss_rate_%. | Use for: item-level margin or spoilage adjustments using loss_rate; category-level aggregations of sales or volume; labeling items with human-friendly names and categories

views.name: shopping_cart_events_ranked
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  visit_id AS visit_id,
  cookie_id AS cookie_id,
  page_id AS page_id,
  event_type AS event_type,
  sequence_number AS sequence_number,
  event_time AS event_time,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY visit_id ORDER BY sequence_number, event_time) AS row_rank
FROM shopping_cart_events

params.description: Provides a per-visit, per-event sequence ranking of shopping cart events: the row number of each event within a visit ordered by sequence_number then event_time.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve ordered events within a visit (e.g., show the Nth event in a visit). | Compose analytics that need event position within a visit (e.g., funnel step ordering, first/last event in a visit). | Join ordered event positions to page or user metadata while preserving per-event order. | Filter or aggregate by event position (e.g., count of first events, distribution of event ranks).
params.output_schema: visit_id: unique identifier of the visit; derived directly from shopping_cart_events.visit_id | cookie_id: identifier for the visitor's cookie; derived directly from shopping_cart_events.cookie_id | page_id: identifier of the page where the event occurred; derived directly from shopping_cart_events.page_id | event_type: type/category of the event (e.g., add_to_cart, view); derived directly from shopping_cart_events.event_type | sequence_number: sequence number provided by the source for ordering events within the visit; derived directly from shopping_cart_events.sequence_number | event_time: timestamp of the event; derived directly from shopping_cart_events.event_time | row_rank: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY visit_id ORDER BY sequence_number, event_time) — 1-based rank of the event within the visit, ties broken by event_time
params.grounded_columns: shopping_cart_events.visit_id | shopping_cart_events.cookie_id | shopping_cart_events.page_id | shopping_cart_events.event_type | shopping_cart_events.sequence_number | shopping_cart_events.event_time
params.metric: row_rank = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shopping_cart_events.visit_id ORDER BY shopping_cart_events.sequence_number, shopping_cart_events.event_time)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension-like, one-row-per-key tables/views on keys that are a superset of this view's grain without duplicating rows: e.g., join to shopping_cart_users_cookie_map on cookie_id — safe because shopping_cart_users_cookie_map is expected to be one-row-per-cookie and this view is one-row-per-(visit_id,sequence_number), so joining on cookie_id will not duplicate the per-event rows (each event row will attach cookie-level attributes). | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to shopping_cart_events_with_page on (visit_id, sequence_number) or on page_id if that view is one-row-per-page_id — safe if the target view/table is one-row-per-key matching the event row; joining on (visit_id, sequence_number) is exact row-level enrichment and will not duplicate measures. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views (e.g., an events-to-actions table that can have multiple child rows per event) without re-aggregating first, because that would multiply this view's rows and any derived counts/measures. If you must join to a one-to-many relation, aggregate the child side to one row per (visit_id, sequence_number) (or per visit_id, depending on your intended grain) before joining. | do NOT join to time-series aggregates that are at a coarser grain (e.g., bitcoin_prices_daily) on only a date key and then attempt to sum row_rank or treat row_rank as a measure — row_rank is positional (not additive) and only meaningful at the event row grain. If combining with coarser aggregates, either (a) keep analytics at the event grain and attach the coarser value as contextual metadata, or (b) aggregate the event rows up (for example count of events by visit or min/max row_rank) before combining with coarser datasets. | When composing metrics: treat row_rank as a positional attribute (dimension). If you need counts or sums per visit, aggregate shopping_cart_events_ranked at the visit level (GROUP BY visit_id) to compute cardinality-safe measures (e.g., events_per_visit = COUNT(*)). | Example safe join keys: (visit_id) to visit-level tables that are one-row-per-visit; (cookie_id) to cookie/user lookup tables that are one-row-per-cookie; (visit_id, sequence_number) to other event-level enriched views that have the exact same event-level grain — these preserve cardinality and do NOT duplicate rows/measures.

views.description: Event-level ranking within a visit ordered by sequence_number and event_time. Exposes a row_rank to allow downstream Top-K sequence filters (e.g., first N events per visit). | Use for: session-first-event or top-N event analyses; ordered funnel steps and transition timing

views.name: bitcoin_transactions_running_totals
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  txn_id AS txn_id,
  member_id AS member_id,
  txn_date AS txn_date,
  txn_time AS txn_time,
  quantity AS quantity,
  SUM(quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY txn_time, txn_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_quantity
FROM bitcoin_transactions

params.description: Provides per-transaction running (cumulative) quantity of bitcoin purchases by member, ordered by transaction time and date.
params.when_to_use: Get the cumulative quantity of bitcoin bought by a member up to and including each transaction (running total) at the transaction grain. | Build reports or timelines that need per-transaction cumulative balance of quantity per member. | Compose further aggregations of cumulative_quantity (e.g., max cumulative per member over a period) or join to transaction-level dimensions without duplicating measures.
params.output_schema: txn_id: unique transaction identifier — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_id | member_id: identifier for the member who made the transaction — derived from bitcoin_transactions.member_id | txn_date: transaction date (calendar date) — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_date | txn_time: transaction timestamp or time used for ordering — derived from bitcoin_transactions.txn_time | quantity: quantity transacted in this transaction (base measure) — derived from bitcoin_transactions.quantity | cumulative_quantity: running total (sum) of quantity for the member up to and including this row, computed with a window function partitioned by member_id ordered by txn_time, txn_date — computed from bitcoin_transactions.quantity via SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY txn_time, txn_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
params.metric: cumulative_quantity = SUM(bitcoin_transactions.quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY bitcoin_transactions.member_id ORDER BY bitcoin_transactions.txn_time, bitcoin_transactions.txn_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) | quantity = bitcoin_transactions.quantity (base measure at txn_id grain)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to one-row-per-member dimension or attributes (e.g., a member_profile view that has one row per member_id) on bitcoin_transactions_running_totals.member_id = member_profile.member_id — safe because bitcoin_transactions_running_totals is one row per txn_id and joining to a single-row-per-member dimension will not duplicate its measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to transaction-level or one-to-one views/tables on txn_id (e.g., detailed transaction metadata keyed by txn_id) — safe because matches are one-to-one so cumulative_quantity remains at transaction grain. | UNSAFE join guidance: do NOT join directly to any one-to-many table or view (for example, a hypothetical transactions_line_items table or any event table with multiple rows per txn_id) without first re-aggregating that table to txn_id grain. Doing so would multiply rows for a single txn_id and thus duplicate cumulative_quantity and quantity measures. If you must combine with a one-to-many table, aggregate that table to txn_id (or member_id with appropriate grouping and use a re-aggregation strategy) before joining. | UNSAFE join guidance: do NOT join to views that expand rows per member (e.g., membership history with multiple rows per member) directly on member_id unless you aggregate or deduplicate the other side to one row per member to avoid inflating cumulative_quantity. | Re-aggregation advice: when composing higher-level metrics (e.g., total cumulative at period end), treat cumulative_quantity as a per-txn snapshot — to compute a member-level cumulative at period cut-off, select the last txn_id/last txn_time per member within the period (or use MAX(cumulative_quantity) after filtering by period) rather than summing cumulative_quantity across transactions (which would double-count). | Ordering note: the running total uses ORDER BY txn_time, txn_date from the base table. If the downstream composition changes ordering semantics (e.g., wants date then time or different tie-breakers), recompute cumulative totals at the desired ordering granularity rather than relying on this view.

views.description: Per-member running total of quantity over time (ordered by txn_time then txn_date) to support cumulative volume and staging for P&L/time-based queries. Preserves txn_id and member_id. | Use for: member cumulative volume and staging for retention cohorts; time-to-threshold analyses using running totals
